    • Support and resistance

    Order block (OB): the last opposite candle before a sharp move

    An order block is the last candle in the opposite direction right before a sharp move that breaks structure. The last down candle before a rise is marked as a bullish OB, the last up candle before a drop as a bearish OB. The range between that candle's high and low becomes an area to watch when price later comes back.

    What is an order block?

    Sometimes price leaves an area very quickly and in one direction. The last candle in the opposite direction right before that sharp move is marked as the place where the move started. That candle is called an order block (OB). The OB zone runs from the candle's high to its low, wicks included.

    The difference from support and resistance is this: support and resistance is an area where price has reacted many times. An OB comes from a single candle and is often a fresh zone that has not been tested again yet.

    The term OB comes from the "Smart Money Concepts" approach. This page treats it as a measurable candle and structure rule.

    Directions

    • Bullish OB: the last down candle before a sharp rise that breaks structure upward. The zone runs from that candle's low to its high.
    • Bearish OB: the last up candle before a sharp drop that breaks structure downward. The zone runs from that candle's high to its low.

    How is it marked?

    Each step gives the bullish OB first, then the bearish OB.

    1. Find the sharp move Look for a move in one direction over several candles, with clearly large bodies. For a bullish OB it is a rise, for a bearish OB a drop.
    2. Check that structure broke The move must break structure with a close (BOS or CHoCH). For a bullish OB the close comes above the previous swing high, for a bearish OB below the previous swing low. A jump or drop that does not break structure does not produce an OB.
    3. Pick the last opposite candle Mark the last opposite candle where the move started. For a bullish OB it is the last down candle; if the next candle went below its low, it is not the last one. For a bearish OB it is the last up candle; if the next candle went above its high, it is not the last one.
    4. Draw the zone The range between the candle's high and low is extended to the right. Until price comes back to it, the zone counts as "untested".

    What makes an OB stronger

    • The move away from the zone is at least twice the height of the OB candle.
    • The move left an FVG behind; price left the zone in one direction, and quickly.
    • The OB is close to an important support or resistance area on a larger timeframe.
    • Price spent little time in the zone; an area where price moved sideways for a long time is not a single OB but a wider supply or demand zone.
    • The zone has not been tested yet. Each new test can weaken its effect.

    These features make the zone more meaningful; they do not guarantee that price will turn there.

    When price comes back

    When price returns to an OB, one of three pictures usually follows. Each card gives the bullish OB first, then the bearish OB.

    Reaction

    Price enters the zone and closes stay inside it. From a bullish OB price rises again (demand), from a bearish OB it falls again (supply).

    Weak reaction

    Price lingers in the zone; rallies from a bullish OB or drops from a bearish OB stay short. Each new touch can weaken the zone a little more.

    Invalidated

    A candle closes beyond the far end of the zone; below the low for a bullish OB, above the high for a bearish OB. The OB is invalidated. The broken zone can later work in the opposite direction; this is called a breaker block.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • Which candle a sharp move started from
    • A fresh zone that can be watched when price comes back
    • That the zone's validity can be measured with a clear closing rule

    What it does not prove

    • That large orders or "smart money" are waiting in the zone
    • That price must come back to the zone
    • That price coming back to the zone must turn there

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    MarketLevelMap's charts do not draw OBs separately yet, but their building blocks are on the page.

    • The BOS and CHoCH labels in the Price Action view show the structure breaks where an OB would be looked for.
    • The FVG boxes in the same view show the gap a sharp move left behind. An OB is often right at the start of that gap.
    • The support and resistance zones on the Critical Zones charts show important areas on larger timeframes. An OB close to one of these zones is more meaningful.

    Timeframes

    On small timeframes OBs form very often and most are short-lived. An OB on a larger timeframe covers a wider area; a narrower OB on a smaller timeframe can sit inside the same zone. That is why an OB is read together with the timeframe it was marked on.

    Often confused with

    • What are support and resistance?Support and resistance is an area where price has reacted many times; an OB comes from a single candle and is often a zone that has not been tested yet.
    • FVG: fair value gapAn FVG is the wick gap a sharp move leaves; an OB is the last opposite candle right before that move. The two often sit side by side.
    • Breaker block: an OB that was closed through and switched rolesA breaker is an OB that was closed through and invalidated, and later works in the opposite direction.

    Key points

    • An OB is the last opposite candle before a sharp move that breaks structure.
    • The zone runs from the candle's high to its low.
    • A close beyond the far end of the zone invalidates the OB.
    • There is no guarantee that an OB will be retested or hold.
